focus: Locate adjacent untrusted-content surfaces in .skilled and map the runtime seam, requirements, measured cost, and risks for default-on integration.
noveltyJustification: Six findings add adjacent prompt-sink evidence and host, provenance, rollout, and privacy requirements; two reinforce the earlier policy-versus-enforcement and measurement limits.
keyQuestions: What drove the measured Jev result?

answeredQuestions: Where else in .skilled would the same judgment pay off?

ruledOut: Treat the deep-research instruction to regard fetched pages as data as equivalent to an enforced fetch-result screen; the same skill says no WebFetch URL/domain allowlist exists, and cli-classifier says no hook is wired.
Reuse the existing Bash/exec dispatch audit as a WebFetch filter without proving the host event and payload contract.
Use Jev's detector verdict as permission to invoke tools or as a substitute for structural metadata controls and code sink review.
focusTrackReason: Iteration 2 recommended locating related untrusted-input judgments in .skilled and mapping the runtime/tool-response seam, requirements, cost, and rollout risks.
partialSuccess: The repository establishes adjacent prompt-sink safeguards but cannot establish WebFetch result-replacement behavior for every installed runtime; that capability and serving cost remain unmeasured.

title: Deep research names fetched pages as untrusted but has no screen wired
claim: The deep-research skill instructs agents to treat WebFetch/WebSearch content as data, not commands, and notes no URL/domain allowlist. The cli-classifier skill says no fetch hook is wired. A retrieval-time verdict can reinforce this policy but cannot replace provenance or instruction hierarchy.

title: Council graph query is a neighboring prompt sink with structural controls
claim: Council artifacts contain user-influenced output that can enter later synthesis prompts. The graph query path responds with an allowlist and bounded strings, so this is a useful adjacent trust boundary where schema and provenance controls should remain primary.

title: Source-to-sink review complements fetched-text screening
claim: The sk-code review playbook requires concrete tracing from untrusted input to SQL, command, path, SSRF, or HTML sinks. Provenance and trust labels can help reviews of external references, but a text classifier cannot replace sink analysis.

title: Feature 035 has no fetch-result serving seam
claim: Feature 035 explicitly adds no hook, settings matcher, or wrapper; the classifier skill also says no verdict is wired to a runtime. The measured keep result is therefore offline and cannot be treated as a default-on runtime control.

title: Default-on needs a per-host pre-context adapter and content provenance
claim: The dispatch catalog documents different event payloads for Bash/exec and audit-only surfaces, not a WebFetch result replacement API. Serving should inspect normalized fetch content before it re-enters model context, carry source and version metadata, and use a fetch/MCP wrapper where a host cannot modify tool results.

title: Keep detection scores separate from permission decisions
claim: The benchmark already reports distinct .25/.50/.75 bands. Use them for annotation, quarantine, or review, and keep deterministic user-intent and runtime-permission checks as independent authorization controls.

title: Serving cost must be measured per real payload
claim: The benchmark makes three classifier calls per row and one auth call; the live receipt is 271 calls for 90 rows with 324 ms p50 and 388 ms p95 call latency. One call per payload or bounded chunk may lower serving call volume, but production latency, tokens, retries, cache behavior, and dollars are unknown.

title: Shadow rollout and explicit unscanned states reduce integration risk
claim: The benchmark used public vendored Markdown sections rather than the longer converted pages selected by an agent. A real-page holdout, hard-benign review, per-host timing tests, privacy/retention rules, and explicit timeout/truncation states are prerequisites before enforcement.
